KV cache eviction policy sensitivity asks: when an inference server must discard cached key-value states to free memory for new requests, which states do you throw away, and how does the answer change when prompts aren't uniform in length, structure, or reuse pattern? The central tension is that most eviction policies (LRU, LFU, prefix-aware caching) were designed with assumptions about prompt regularity — system prompts are stable, user turns are short, document prefixes repeat. When those assumptions break, as in retrieval-augmented generation with variable-length retrieved chunks, multi-turn agents with diverging histories, or batched inference across heterogeneous workloads, eviction decisions that look locally optimal destroy globally valuable cached states, forcing expensive KV recomputation that degrades latency non-linearly because attention cost scales quadratically with sequence length.

What a beginner misses is that cache miss cost is not uniform: evicting a 200-token system prompt prefix and a 4,000-token document encoding are both "one eviction event" in naive accounting, but the recomputation costs differ by 400× — and downstream queued requests that share that document prefix all simultaneously suffer the miss, creating latency spikes that look like thundering herd problems rather than cache policy failures. Experts also worry about the interaction between eviction policy and batching strategy: continuous batching schedulers make eviction decisions implicitly through request ordering, so a policy that seems sound in isolation can produce pathological interference patterns when the prompt length distribution has high variance, particularly heavy tails from long-document or code-generation workloads.

The critical structural property is the prefix tree depth-to-branching-ratio: how deep the shared prefix runs before the distribution fans out into distinct suffixes, relative to how many distinct continuations exist at each branching point. LRU performs near-optimally when this ratio is high — a deep shared trunk with few branches, as in a single-system-prompt chatbot where 90%+ of tokens are identical across requests — because recency correlates tightly with reuse probability. It becomes catastrophic when the ratio inverts: shallow shared prefixes with explosive branching, which is exactly the structure of RAG workloads where a short system prompt is followed by unique per-request retrieved documents, each thousands of tokens long. In that regime, every request looks equally "recent" at the branch point, so LRU has no signal to distinguish a prefix that 500 queued requests will need from one that will never be seen again. SGLang's RadixAttention (2024) exploits the high-ratio case explicitly — it builds a radix tree over cached KV states and evicts leaves first, which is correct when the tree is deep and narrow but degrades to essentially random eviction when the tree is wide and shallow. vLLM's prefix caching similarly assumes that matched prefixes are worth retaining, but under high-branching RAG distributions, prefix match rates drop to near zero and the cache becomes pure overhead, a phenomenon the PagedAttention paper does not analyze because its evaluation workloads lacked realistic retrieval-induced variance.

Under block-based allocation (vLLM uses 16-token pages by default), a heavy-tailed length distribution creates asymmetric fragmentation pressure: median-length requests consume predictable, compact block counts, but a single 95th-percentile request arriving mid-batch can instantaneously claim 10× the block budget, forcing the eviction of dozens of cached prefixes to satisfy one allocation — a fragmentation pattern that hit-rate metrics average away because the eviction burst is temporally concentrated and statistically rare. The deeper problem is internal fragmentation at block boundaries: a 4,097-token prompt wastes nearly a full 16-token block on its final page, and when you have many long requests simultaneously, the wasted tail-blocks can consume 5-15% of total cache capacity without appearing as misses in any standard metric. This interacts with eviction policy through what you might call eviction volume asymmetry: LRU and LFU count eviction events, but one eviction of a long-document KV block frees 16 tokens worth of space — potentially forcing hundreds of subsequent small evictions to free enough contiguous (or logically groupable) blocks to satisfy the next large allocation. The SGLang and vLLM teams both report that under production RAG workloads, the metric that actually predicts user-visible latency degradation is not cache hit rate but recomputation FLOP rate — the total floating point operations spent regenerating evicted KV states — because this captures the length-weighted cost that hit rate treats uniformly. A further hidden interaction: eviction of a long prefix mid-generation (to free blocks for a new arrival) doesn't just cause a miss — in systems without swap-to-CPU, it can force preemption and full request restart, converting a cache miss into a latency multiplier of 3-8× for the victimized request, a phenomenon Sarathi-Serve (2023) specifically targets with chunked prefill to reduce the block pressure spikes that trigger these cascades.

When you switch to recomputation FLOP rate, the failure mode that surfaces is decode-phase KV eviction cascade: a request that has already completed prefill and is mid-decode still holds KV blocks for its entire context, and under memory pressure those blocks are candidates for eviction in systems that don't distinguish between "cached for future reuse" and "actively needed for current generation." Hit rate metrics miss this entirely because the evicted blocks belong to an in-flight request, not a prefix cache entry — there is no "miss" recorded, only a preemption event that may be logged separately or not at all. The recomputation FLOP metric exposes this because preempting a request at decode step 200 of a 2,000-step generation means recomputing the entire prefill KV state from scratch — potentially 50-200 TFLOP for a long-context request — dwarfing the cost of any prefix cache miss in the system. The pathological interaction is priority inversion under continuous batching: the scheduler admits a new high-priority long-prompt request, which triggers eviction of blocks from a nearly-finished decode-phase request to satisfy prefill memory demand, and the preempted request re-enters the queue behind the new arrival, potentially being preempted again if the memory pressure is sustained — a livelock that Orca (2022) and subsequent systems acknowledge but don't fully solve without explicit preemption budgets. Sarathi-Serve's chunked prefill partially addresses this by spreading new-request prefill across multiple scheduling steps, reducing the block-demand spike, but the fundamental tension remains: decode-phase blocks are simultaneously "actively used" and "eviction targets" in any system without explicit residency pinning, and recomputation FLOP rate is the only metric sensitive enough to detect when this tension is causing repeated preemption of the same request.

Since decode-phase blocks must be pinned to prevent cascade preemption, but pinning reduces the evictable pool available to absorb new arrivals, what is the correct optimization target for a pinning policy — and how does the answer change when you have SLA latency percentile commitments versus pure throughput maximization?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2985)

Under pure throughput maximization, the correct optimization target for a pinning policy is minimizing total recomputation FLOPs per unit time, which means pinning blocks only when the expected recomputation cost of eviction exceeds the opportunity cost of blocking new request admission — concretely, you pin a decode-phase request's blocks only if its remaining decode steps times per-step memory bandwidth cost exceeds the prefill FLOP cost of the new arrival waiting for those blocks. This leads to a completion-proximity heuristic: requests within some threshold of finishing (say, >80% of estimated decode steps complete) get pinned because their blocks will be freed imminently anyway, while early-decode requests are eviction candidates since requeuing them costs less than stalling a large incoming prefill — a policy approximated by the "last-come-first-evict among decode-phase" strategy discussed in the Preble (2024) multi-instance serving paper. Under SLA latency percentile commitments, the optimization target inverts in a subtle way: you are no longer minimizing average recomputation cost but bounding tail latency, which means the pinning policy must account for the fact that a preempted request's requeue latency is unbounded if the system remains under sustained pressure — one preemption can cascade into three or four if memory never clears, blowing a P99 SLA even when P50 looks healthy. This forces a more conservative pinning policy — pin all decode-phase blocks once a request has passed a much earlier threshold, perhaps 30-40% completion — accepting lower raw throughput to prevent the tail-latency explosions that SLA contracts price at penalty rates orders of magnitude above average-case cost. The practical conflict is that SLA-driven pinning under heavy load can cause admission starvation: the evictable pool shrinks to near zero as most in-flight requests become pinned, forcing the scheduler to queue new arrivals rather than admit them, which moves the latency problem from existing requests to new ones and can violate time-to-first-token SLAs even while protecting generation-completion SLAs — a tradeoff that systems like Llumnix (2024) attempt to escape through live KV migration across instances rather than local eviction alone.

The core consistency hazard is migrating-state divergence: if the decode loop continues advancing on the source instance during migration, each new decode step appends fresh KV vectors for the newly generated token to the source's block set, but those vectors are not yet on the destination — so the destination receives a snapshot of KV state that is already stale by the time transfer completes, and the number of stale steps equals migration latency divided by per-step decode time. For a 7B model on A100 serving a 4,000-token context, a single decode step takes roughly 20-30ms under moderate batch load, and PCIe-based inter-node KV transfer for that context runs 50-150ms depending on block count, meaning the destination can be 3-7 tokens behind the source at handoff — those tokens must either be recomputed on the destination or buffered and replayed, and neither option is free. Llumnix handles this with a pause-and-copy final delta approach: it copies the bulk of KV blocks while decode continues, then briefly pauses the source decode loop, transfers the delta blocks generated during migration, and resumes on the destination — but this pause introduces a latency bubble that violates the decode step regularity that downstream token streaming clients expect, potentially triggering client-side timeout logic tuned to per-step latency. A subtler hazard is attention mask consistency: the KV blocks on the source accumulate position embeddings and causal mask state implicitly through the order of block allocation; if the destination reassembles blocks in a different physical order (which block-based allocators permit since logical sequence is tracked separately), and any indexing bug exists in the position remapping, the model silently attends to tokens in wrong positions — producing plausible but factually corrupted output with no error signal. The deepest problem is that these consistency windows make migration atomicity impossible without stopping decode, so all practical systems (Llumnix, and the disaggregated prefill-decode architecture in Splitwise 2024) instead treat migration as an approximation and rely on the delta-replay window being short enough that recomputation cost is negligible — an assumption that breaks under high batch load precisely when migration is most needed, creating a consistency-vs-efficiency coupling that has no clean resolution within a single-model-instance architecture.

Disaggregated prefill-decode does not solve the migration consistency hazard — it relocates it to the prefill-to-decode KV transfer boundary, which is now a permanent architectural interface rather than an occasional migration event, meaning the consistency problem must be solved correctly every request rather than only during load-spike migrations. The exact point where consistency must be enforced is the last-token-of-prefill / first-token-of-decode handoff: the prefill instance must signal that KV block production is complete and the blocks are coherent before the decode instance issues its first autoregressive step, because if the decode instance begins sampling before all prefill KV blocks are durably transferred, it attends over an incomplete context and the error is undetectable — the model produces fluent but contextually truncated output. Splitwise (2024) enforces this with an explicit transfer completion barrier: the prefill instance writes KV blocks to shared GPU memory or RDMA fabric, then sends a completion token to the decode instance's scheduler, and decode does not begin until that token is received — but this barrier is now on the critical path of every request, and under RDMA contention or NVLink saturation the barrier wait can consume 10-40ms, negating much of the latency benefit of separation for short-context requests. The relocated hazard has a new failure mode that didn't exist in unified architectures: partial transfer visibility, where the interconnect delivers KV blocks out of order and the decode instance's block allocator, if it lacks sequence-number validation, can begin decode with a complete block count but incorrect block contents for the layers transferred last — a bug class that unified systems never encounter because prefill and decode share the same physical memory. DistServe (2024) addresses this by treating the KV transfer as an ordered stream with layer-granularity sequence numbers, but this adds per-layer synchronization overhead and means the effective barrier is not one signal but N signals for N transformer layers, serially gating decode start — so the disaggregated architecture has traded one hard consistency problem for N smaller ones whose cumulative latency cost must be benchmarked against the parallelism gains to determine whether separation is actually worthwhile for a given context length and model depth.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2988)

The arithmetic favors co-location when prefill-to-decode token ratio is low — concretely, when the average request has a short prompt and a long generation, the KV transfer cost is small (few blocks to move) but the decode phase is long, so disaggregation's benefit of freeing prefill compute for other requests is real; conversely, when prompts are long and generations are short (summarization, classification, RAG answer extraction), the transfer cost is high relative to decode duration and co-location wins because the barrier latency exceeds the parallelism gain. DistServe's own evaluation shows the crossover empirically: for prompt lengths above roughly 2,000 tokens with output lengths below 200 tokens, disaggregated architectures show worse P99 TTFT than co-located ones on the same hardware budget, because the RDMA transfer of a 2,000-token, 32-layer KV state at 40GB/s takes ~25ms, which exceeds the decode phase entirely for a 100-token output at 20ms/step. The phase boundary workload characteristic is therefore the ratio of prefill FLOPs to total request FLOPs — call it the prefill fraction φ: when φ is high (approaching 1, as in long-prompt short-output workloads), disaggregation moves the bottleneck onto the interconnect without meaningfully parallelizing the dominant cost; when φ is low (long multi-turn generation, creative writing, code synthesis), disaggregation lets prefill instances pipeline across many requests while decode instances run continuously, and the transfer cost is amortized over hundreds of decode steps. A second workload characteristic that shifts the boundary is request arrival burstiness: under bursty traffic, disaggregated systems can independently scale prefill instance count to absorb prompt spikes without over-provisioning decode capacity, a flexibility co-located systems cannot exploit — so the same mean φ can favor different architectures depending on coefficient of variation in arrival rate, which is why Splitwise reports 30% cost reduction on production traffic (which is bursty) despite mixed φ values. The underappreciated boundary condition is model size relative to interconnect bandwidth: for a 70B model where a single layer's KV state per token is ~1MB, the transfer arithmetic degrades faster with prompt length than for a 7B model, meaning the co-location crossover prompt length drops from ~2,000 tokens to ~400 tokens — so the architecture choice that is correct for a 7B deployment can be actively harmful for a 70B deployment serving the same workload distribution.
